masthead_title: Nvidia's board brought Jensen Huang back as CEO, and the S&P 500 just posted its best day since April 2025, pulling the index out of its correction.
regime_line: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, and the S&P 500 jumped 4.73% — its best single day since April 2025 — pulling the index out of correction territory, even though credit spreads haven't had a chance yet to weigh in on the move.
claims_section_html:
Claims ledger — one confirms today, one still open

CL-0072 (Wednesday's hawkish FOMC minutes marking a genuine new leg of the dollar's climb, not a one-day reaction) — confirmed. All three test sessions are in: DXY closed at or above Wednesday 11-18's 103.86 baseline on two of the three (Thursday 11-19: 103.90; Monday 11-23: 104.32), clearing the “at least 2 of 3” confirm bar, and never touched the 103.49 refute line (the window's low was Friday 11-20's 103.81). The dollar's post-minutes climb held as an independent new leg, not a one-day reaction to the minutes text.

CL-0073 (Thursday's broad four-way risk-off agreement marking a genuine extension of the selloff, not a one-day echo of Anthropic's debut volatility) — not due until 2026-11-25. Two of its three sessions are in, and today's bounce worked against it: Friday's S&P 500 close (6,910.39) was below the 7,175.83 confirm reference, but Monday's rally carried the index back above it (7,237.17) — only 1 of 2 sessions so far counts toward the “at least 2 of 3 below” confirm bar, and tomorrow's close now has to do all the remaining work. Credit (HY/IG OAS) is still flagged on both legs, but the refute path (S&P at or above $7,369 with both credit series easing below |z| 1.5) didn't fire today either.
story_html:
Monday was this run's biggest rally yet. The S&P 500 rose 4.73% to 7,237.17, the Nasdaq Composite rose 6.51% to 24,089.56, and the Russell 2000 rose 3.40% to 2,669.66 — all after Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO (Form 8-K, 2026-11-23), eleven days after the board had accepted his resignation and said it had no plans to bring him back (South China Morning Post). Nvidia itself rose 31.48% to $165.05, adding back nearly $1 trillion in market value in a single session (Fool.com, Yahoo Finance), and the rally spread across the whole chip/AI-hardware complex — Dell +20.46%, Micron +19.04%, Marvell +18.37%, and well over a hundred other names (Movers, below). Technology (XLK, +8.97%) was the day's largest sector divergence from the market (SPY, +4.71%), by 4.26 points; Energy (XLE, −1.06%) and Consumer Staples (XLP, −0.09%) were the only two sector ETFs to fall. The move pulled the S&P 500 back to 7.44% below its October 6 record — out of the confirmed-correction territory (10%+ off the high) this brief noted Friday's 11.62% reading had reached.

This system's own pull confirms the headline but adds two wrinkles before calling this a clean reversal. First, the rally was narrow, not broad: SPY rose 4.71% while the equal-weight RSP rose only 2.59%, a 2.1-point gap (breadth, Concept below) — most of today's gain sat in a cluster of AI-linked mega-caps, not across the average stock, the same concentration this system found in October's selloff, just running the other way. Second, credit hasn't voted yet: HY and IG OAS are both still dated Friday 11-20 (the usual one-session publication lag) at 3.76% and 0.98%, both still flagged near their widest levels this run has seen — not because credit disagrees with today's rally, but because today's own print won't arrive until tomorrow. The dollar, the fourth hierarchy vote, kept climbing anyway (DXY +0.49% to 104.32, still flagged, CL-0072 confirmed above) — a reminder that not every part of the picture joined today's rally. Treasury yields, for their part, barely moved. The 10-year held at 4.92%. The 30-year eased 2bp to 5.29%, a level it last touched, before this run, briefly, in June 2007 (History, below). Rates simply sat out today's equity story. One sharp divergence inside the rally itself: CrowdStrike fell 8.92% the same morning it reported a record quarter and announced an all-stock deal to acquire rival Zscaler (Movers, below) — idiosyncratic to that one deal, not part of the broader AI-hardware move.
dashboard_interp_html:
Treasury yields were mostly quiet while stocks did the moving. The 3-month bill rose 5bp to 4.37% (z +1.92, flagged; 54th percentile since the early 1980s, 73rd of the last 30 years) — the one tenor that actually moved, a front-end-only wrinkle with no story behind it in today's pull. The 2-year held flat at 4.63% (z +0.74, below the flag line; 50th percentile over the full ~50-year record but the 79th of the last 30 years, † a 29-point gap). The 10-year held flat at 4.92% (z +0.47; 46th/82nd %ile, †). The 30-year eased 2bp to 5.29% (z +0.27; 46th/81st %ile, † — today's lead History-check fact, below: before this run, this level was last touched, briefly, in June 2007). The curve barely moved (2s10s unchanged at 29bp, z −1.19; 3m10y flattened 5bp to 55bp, z −2.01, flagged) on the front end's small rise. Why this matters: a bond is a loan, and when nearly the whole curve sits still on a day stocks jump almost 5%, that's a sign today's rally was a stock-specific story, not a change in the rate outlook that bond investors are reacting to.

Credit and the dollar told a different story — partly because credit hasn't caught up to today yet. HY OAS — the extra yield investors demand to lend to junk-rated companies over safe Treasurys — held at 3.76% (dated Friday 11-20, the usual one-session lag; z +3.18, flagged; 96th percentile of its own ~3-year record, marked * since this live series has no multi-decade history, §4F). IG OAS, the investment-grade equivalent, held at 0.98% (also dated Friday; z +3.06, flagged; 87th percentile of its own ~3-year record, marked *). Both numbers predate today's rally entirely — they can't yet say whether credit agrees with it. The dollar (DXY) rose 0.49% to 104.32 (z +2.74, this run's largest Tier 1 flag on a running basis; 76th percentile over the full ~55-year dollar record and the 86th of the last 30 years) — unlike credit, the dollar's own number is live as of today, and it kept climbing even as stocks rallied. Gold rose 3.87% to $3,651.40 but stayed flagged (z −2.71, a third straight flagged session) and copper rose 2.74% to $5.627/lb but stayed even more deeply flagged (z −3.40, this run's largest |z| of any series today, Chart of the day below) — both bounced today, but not enough to offset five weeks of decline before it. Why this matters: when a flag barely moves on a big reversal day, check the calendar on the data before reading it as disagreement — sometimes the number just hasn't had its turn yet.
history_html:
Today's deepest echo is still the 30-year Treasury, now at 5.29%, first reaching this level Aug 17 and there on 47 of the 68 sessions since — not every session. Before this run, the last time was June 2007, and only briefly (2 sessions); this run's own high, 5.67% on Oct 7, was last matched in July 2001. The two lenses disagree: 81st percentile of the last 30 years, just 46th since 1977 — unusual lately, unremarkable historically (every 1980s reading sat at or above today's 5.29%). The then-vs-now panel below shows where June 2007 and today line up — not on policy: 2007's Fed was near a cyclical peak; today's isn't.

Second: the 10-year TIPS real yield (2.77%, dated Friday) sits at the 99th percentile of its own 24-year record, there on 25 of the last 40 sessions since Sep. 24. Before this run, last reached November 2008, inside the 2007-09 financial crisis, and only briefly. The Cleveland Fed's longer model, back to 1982, reads milder — 81st of the last 30 years, just 54th since 1982 — TIPS alone are too short a history to call this extreme on their own.

Third: the S&P 500's 4.73% gain is a move of a size that comes about 27 times in the last 30 years — roughly once a year — and it's the first this year; the last one at least this big was April 9, 2025, when markets rallied on President Trump's announced 90-day tariff pause (Axios, Yahoo Finance), a very different trigger than one company's CEO news. Client-ready: two Tier 1 readings — the 30-year Treasury and the 10-year real yield — are still echoing 2007-09 crisis-era levels even after today's bounce, but the backdrop differs from both; the echo is in the level, not the cause.
movers_html:
How this section works: all 503 S&P constituents scanned mechanically, plus the top-50 megacaps; a stock qualifies only by moving >4% (>2.5% for the 50 biggest) or a sector ETF diverging ≥1.5pp from SPX, never by seeming interesting. 150 name candidates qualified today (up from 116 Friday) and 7 sector ETFs cleared the divergence bar (the same as Friday). Earnings/guidance reactions are prioritized per §5; CrowdStrike reported its own Q3 results today and is covered for that reason. Nvidia is covered first as today's clear catalyst. Also qualifying, left out under the cap: MU (+19.04%), MRVL (+18.37%), LITE (+18.21%), BE (+18.09%), HPE (+17.38%), MPWR (+16.80%), INTC (+16.34%), COHR (+15.27%), KLAC (+14.96%), GLW (+14.76%) — not individually researched today given the cap; none asserted to lack a catalyst, simply not checked.

Nvidia (NVDA) +31.48% (165.05, from 125.53) — what happened: the company's board reinstated Jensen Huang as president, CEO, and board director (Form 8-K, 2026-11-23), eleven days after accepting his Nov. 12 resignation and naming CFO Colette Kress interim CEO. Stated reason: per the company's own filing and reporting (South China Morning Post, Fool.com), the board held a series of discussions with Huang and said it was satisfied with his candor and ability to lead; it said it received input from senior levels of the U.S. government and concluded reinstatement poses no national-security risk; an independent committee's investigation into reports Huang was the target of a foreign-intelligence effort continues, and Huang says he supports it. Read-through: directly Tier 3-relevant — the single largest driver of today's chip/AI-hardware rally, and the clearest live test yet of whether the Nov. 5-started AI-capex-doubt selloff (this run's dominant theme for three weeks, CL-0070/CL-0071) was about demand and financing fundamentals or about leadership uncertainty at the sector's bellwether.

Dell Technologies (DELL) +20.46% (334.91, from 278.02) — what happened: rose alongside the broader chip/AI-server complex, with no company-specific news of its own found in today's search. Stated reason: per Fool.com's and Yahoo Finance's same-day coverage, the rally across chip and AI-infrastructure names tracked directly to Nvidia's reinstatement news, not to anything specific to Dell. Read-through: sympathy, not idiosyncratic — a clean read on how far AI-capex-doubt sentiment had spread beyond Nvidia itself, and how quickly it reversed on one piece of leadership news.

CrowdStrike (CRWD) −8.92% (208.97, from 229.44) — what happened: fell the same morning it reported Q3 FY2027 results (a record quarter, including net new ARR of $419 million) and announced a definitive agreement to acquire rival Zscaler in an all-stock deal (1.135 CrowdStrike shares per Zscaler share), per its own Form 8-K. Stated reason: no named outlet in today's search specifically tied the stock's drop to the deal's terms or the earnings print; reported as such rather than inferred. Read-through: idiosyncratic to CrowdStrike's own M&A/earnings day — no read-through to the broader AI-hardware story.
chart_of_day_why: Copper carries this run's single largest |z| of any series today at −3.40, just ahead of HY OAS (+3.18) and IG OAS (+3.06) — the mechanical pick by rule (a), even though copper itself rose 2.74% today. Five weeks of decline from an early-November high stretched the 120-day average and spread so far that one green session barely moves the z-score, a live illustration of the same mechanic gold showed Friday.
tier3_html:
Daily read: SMH outperformed SPY by 10.32 percentage points today (+15.03% vs. +4.71%) — a mirror-image reversal of Friday's −6.96-point gap in the other direction (Movers/Story, above). Nvidia's reinstatement news is the clear, named driver behind the chip/AI-hardware complex specifically outrunning the broader rally, not a diffuse risk-on move across every sector (Energy and Consumer Staples were the only two sectors lower today).

Weekly issuance/spread note: no fresh, dated hyperscaler-issuance or vendor-financing news surfaced in today's search beyond what's already in recent briefs. This week's own HY/IG OAS prints (Dashboard, above) are still dated Friday and haven't yet reflected today's rally; Friday 2026-11-27 (a holiday-shortened half day) is the next scheduled Tier 3 weekly depth section.
calendar_note_html:
Today: CB Consumer Confidence (cons. 92.1, prior 91.7), 10:00am ET, is the session's only medium-impact release; the Richmond Fed Manufacturing Index (cons. −3, prior −2) and the S&P/Case-Shiller home-price index are low-impact. Tomorrow, Wednesday 11-25, carries this week's real test: Core PCE (the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, cons. +0.3% m/m) and the preliminary Q3 GDP print (cons. +3.5%), both 8:30am ET and high-impact — also the day CL-0073 (Flags, below) comes due. Markets are closed Thursday for Thanksgiving with a half day Friday, so Wednesday's releases are effectively this week's last full data read before the holiday.

Why this matters to the current regime: today's own calendar is light enough that the rally runs largely undisturbed by new data; tomorrow's Core PCE/GDP pair is the first real test of whether the growth-and-inflation backdrop still supports a rally this concentrated, once rates, credit, and tomorrow's overdue OAS fill all have a chance to weigh in.
concept_unit: Unit 6 — Positioning & sentiment vs. fundamentals, segment 4 reinforcement (R)
concept_title: A rally can be just as narrow as a selloff — today's bounce, by the numbers
concept_html:
Segment 4 taught that the same breadth tool used to spot a concentrated selloff works just as well on a green day: compare the cap-weighted index to the equal-weight average. If the cap-weighted index rises a lot more than the average, the gains sat in a handful of giant stocks, not across the market. Today is close to a textbook case. SPY rose 4.71% while the equal-weight RSP rose only 2.59% — a 2.1-point gap. The Russell 2000, a pure small-cap gauge, rose 3.40%, in between the two. All three numbers are positive, but the gap says this bounce wasn't evenly shared: a cluster of AI-linked mega-caps — Nvidia foremost — did most of the lifting.

Why this matters: a narrow rally can fade faster than a broad one, because it depends on a smaller number of stocks continuing to lead. It doesn't mean today's move was fake — real money moved real prices — it means the bounce is still concentrated, the same way October's selloff was.
client_translation: Today's big rally was real, but it was driven mostly by a handful of giant tech stocks bouncing back — not by the whole market joining in equally, which is worth knowing before assuming every account recovered the same amount today.
client_lens_html:
“Did you see Nvidia today? Is the AI selloff over?” Nvidia's board brought Jensen Huang back as CEO, and the whole chip/AI-hardware group rallied hard with it — the S&P 500 is back out of its correction (7.44% off its October record, versus 11.62% on Friday). But credit spreads (HY and IG OAS) are still showing Friday's stressed reading because today's own number hasn't arrived yet — worth saying “we'll know more once credit weighs in” rather than calling this settled.

“Was today's rally broad, or just a few big stocks?” Mostly a few big stocks. The S&P 500 ETF (SPY) rose 4.71% while the equal-weight average (RSP) rose only 2.59% — a real but concentrated bounce, led by AI-linked names, the same pattern (in reverse) that drove October's selloff (Concept, above).

“What happened with CrowdStrike and Zscaler?” CrowdStrike agreed to buy security rival Zscaler in an all-stock deal the same morning it reported a record quarter, and its own stock fell nearly 9% even as the rest of the market rallied — a reminder that one company's acquisition can move its stock in the opposite direction from everything else, for reasons specific to that one deal.
